title: Smith et al. (2007): Multiple-Choice Quiz
instructions: Choose the single best answer. Focus on the meanings of the interview accounts, the distinction between participant statements and interpretation, and the limits of a qualitative substudy. Assistance can support independence as well as challenge it.

items.prompt: Which statement best captures the paper's central argument?
options: Independence has one fixed meaning and produces the same health risks in all older men.
Successful aging is a purely biological state with no connection to masculine identities.
Independence draws on intertwined discourses of masculinity and successful aging, shaping help seeking.
Help seeking depends on medical knowledge alone and is unrelated to how independence is understood.
items.answer: Independence draws on intertwined discourses of masculinity and successful aging, shaping help seeking.
items.explanation: The authors argue that masculinity and successful-aging discourses are intertwined in the men's accounts of independence. Independence can involve avoiding help, but also maintaining daily function and quality of life. Understanding those meanings can inform how health services engage older men; the paper does not establish a single universal effect.

items.prompt: How does the introduction characterize independence within hegemonic masculinity?
options: It is a fixed biological trait defined entirely by physical strength, excluding cultural and relational variation.
It privileges self-reliance and autonomy, while meanings of masculinity can vary across cultures and settings.
It defines frequent requests for help as the only culturally accepted form of masculine behavior in every setting.
It is an individual personality trait that first appears in old age and remains separate from social expectations.
items.answer: It privileges self-reliance and autonomy, while meanings of masculinity can vary across cultures and settings.
items.explanation: The introduction describes a culturally influential model that privileges self-reliance and autonomy. It also discusses critiques of a single hegemonic model and the variation of masculinities across environments and cultures. The account therefore concerns social expectations, not a biological rule that describes every man.

items.prompt: How does the paper complicate the relationship between independence and successful aging?
options: Success depends entirely on one physical-function score, regardless of self-determination, personal meanings, or culture.
Different forms of reliance and autonomy can coexist on a continuum, and ideas of success are culturally shaped.
Any help from another person eliminates independence and must be classified as failure, regardless of retained abilities.
Independence means only living in a separate household and excludes purpose, self-esteem, and continuity of identity.
items.answer: Different forms of reliance and autonomy can coexist on a continuum, and ideas of success are culturally shaped.
items.explanation: Reliance on others does not automatically imply unsuccessful aging. The authors describe varied forms of dependence and levels of independence, and discuss autonomy, purpose, personal growth, self-esteem, and continuity of self. They caution against a simple success–failure judgment detached from cultural and personal meanings.

items.prompt: Which description identifies the qualitative substudy used in this paper?
options: All 1,195 men in the full FAMAS cohort, each contributing repeated qualitative interviews.
Only the 22 men in the older age strata, with younger participants excluded from the substudy.
Twelve couples consisting of men aged 65 or older and their partners, interviewed as dyads.
Thirty-six men invited using age and marital-status strata from the wider FAMAS cohort.
items.answer: Thirty-six men invited using age and marital-status strata from the wider FAMAS cohort.
items.explanation: The full FAMAS cohort contained 1,195 men aged 35–80, whereas this qualitative substudy involved 36. The paper primarily draws on the understandings of the older 22 participants, including 12 aged 65 or older, but also presents some middle-aged men's accounts. The larger cohort's longitudinal design does not make the interview analysis a longitudinal test.

items.prompt: Which description matches the interview setting and conduct?
options: Four researchers each conducted two-hour sessions at a university, with spouses present during every morning interview.
All interviews took place in outpatient clinics, lasted half an hour, and required participants' partners to attend.
All interviews were short telephone calls, so the study recorded neither physical setting nor participants' preferences.
JS conducted 60–105-minute interviews, mostly at home in the afternoon or evening, with alternatives requested by participants.
items.answer: JS conducted 60–105-minute interviews, mostly at home in the afternoon or evening, with alternatives requested by participants.
items.explanation: The first author conducted every interview. Most took place at participants' homes, often at times they requested. Four used a university room or workplace at participants' request. The authors chose settings intended to avoid threats to masculine identity; this is part of the reported research context, not proof that one setting works for every man.

items.prompt: How did the authors interpret the age difference between JS and many participants?
options: It prompted comparisons with earlier life experiences, creating opportunities to explore health and masculinity across the life course.
It made every account of depression, sexual concerns, or emotional expression unreliable and required excluding those topics.
It was irrelevant to interviewing because the researchers treated participants and interviewer as members of the same generation.
It served only as an independent variable for calculating a statistical effect of age on the number of health-service visits.
items.answer: It prompted comparisons with earlier life experiences, creating opportunities to explore health and masculinity across the life course.
items.explanation: JS was 25 and most participants were in older age groups. Men sometimes compared his age with their own earlier experiences, giving opportunities to probe life-course narratives. This is reflexive discussion of how accounts were produced, not evidence from repeated measurements of the same men over decades.

items.prompt: How were the interview materials processed and analyzed?
options: Selected passages were summarized and classified under fixed hypotheses before response frequencies were tested.
Responses became numerical scores used to estimate effects as if participants had been randomly assigned to care.
Verbatim transcripts and relevant field notes were coded in NVIVO and analyzed through inductive thematic analysis.
Clinical diagnoses and prescription records alone were compared to calculate differences in disease prevalence.
items.answer: Verbatim transcripts and relevant field notes were coded in NVIVO and analyzed through inductive thematic analysis.
items.explanation: JS transcribed the interviews verbatim, added field notes where necessary, and coded the material with NVIVO using an inductive approach to thematic analysis. The software supported coding; it did not itself establish causal effects, population prevalence, or the validity of an interpretation.

items.prompt: How did the authors interpret one man's emphasis on controlling diabetes and another's emphasis on staying strong during illness?
options: These accounts combine masculine self-sufficiency with concerns about maintaining a good life while aging.
Both men surrendered all health decisions to clinicians and rejected having any personal control over illness.
Both defined independence solely as maintaining income, without referring to their health or daily experience.
The accounts demonstrate that one man sought immediate help while the other permanently stopped exercising.
items.answer: These accounts combine masculine self-sufficiency with concerns about maintaining a good life while aging.
items.explanation: The accounts attributed to Conrad and Harry emphasize control and strength. The authors place these themes within intertwined discourses: independence marks masculine identity and the capacity to maintain quality of life as men age. The interpretations should not be reduced to either discourse alone.

items.prompt: What interpretation fits accounts of resisting reliance despite a wife's involvement or feeling burdensome when help was available?
options: The men always accepted family advice immediately and never experienced tension between self-reliance and seeking help.
Fees and travel distance alone determined their behavior; perceived burden and personal meanings of independence played no role.
Preserving self-reliance and avoiding a sense of burden could discourage help seeking even within supportive relationships.
All the men lived alone without available assistance, so family and household relationships were absent from the analysis.
items.answer: Preserving self-reliance and avoiding a sense of burden could discourage help seeking even within supportive relationships.
items.explanation: Sam and Ben described wives' involvement alongside their preference to manage matters themselves. Arnold described not calling an available lodger after a fall because he felt he might burden others. These accounts illustrate perceived barriers to seeking help, without showing that every older man or every family responds in the same way.

items.prompt: Why did the authors interpret a man's refusal of community nursing as more than simple stubbornness?
options: They treated refusal as diagnostic evidence of cognitive impairment shared by older men generally.
His account linked a long history of self-care to both masculine identity and concerns about aging.
They treated the refusal as an irrelevant joke and removed it from their analysis of health-service use.
They attributed it solely to family coercion and excluded the man's own explanation of independence.
items.answer: His account linked a long history of self-care to both masculine identity and concerns about aging.
items.explanation: Max first described himself as stubborn, then explained how long he had looked after himself and his fears about losing that capacity. The authors use this shift to connect masculinity with aging and continuity of an independent life. Understanding that context is distinct from proving that delaying needed help is beneficial.

items.prompt: What understanding of independence appears in the accounts of maintaining self-care and physical or cognitive functioning?
options: The only measure of success is the longest possible survival, regardless of enjoyment or the ability to act.
Daily functioning can be preserved only by rejecting every kind of help from family members and clinicians.
A full life and the capacity to do valued activities matter alongside, rather than simply extending, lifespan.
Only continued paid employment can demonstrate good health, while self-care and chosen activities are irrelevant.
items.answer: A full life and the capacity to do valued activities matter alongside, rather than simply extending, lifespan.
items.explanation: David emphasized being able to care for himself and do what he wanted, while Bob emphasized physical and cognitive functioning. Their accounts link independence to quality of life. These examples include middle-aged participants, showing why the qualitative sample should not be described as exclusively aged 65 or older.
items.source: Findings: daily function and quality of life

items.prompt: What shared concern connects an account of threatened eyesight with another of needing help with basic personal care?
options: Both men valued accurately predicting and maximizing survival above all concerns about daily function and dependence.
Reading and driving mattered only for income and were unrelated to the men's independence or quality of life.
Serious illness removed all concerns about dependence and led both men to focus exclusively on living longer.
Valued daily activities and concerns about relying on others shaped what made continued life meaningful.
items.answer: Valued daily activities and concerns about relying on others shaped what made continued life meaningful.
items.explanation: Wayne discussed reading and driving as reasons eyesight mattered; Roger feared losing basic self-care and becoming a burden. The authors interpret these accounts as focusing attention on quality of life as well as survival. They report participants' meanings rather than endorsing a judgment that dependent lives lack value.
items.source: Findings: functional loss and perceived quality of life

items.prompt: How should participant report and researcher interpretation be separated in the driving-licence case?
options: Licence loss and distress were reported directly; a loss of masculine identity was the authors' qualified interpretation.
The participant denied cognitive difficulties and explicitly said that losing his licence had improved his quality of life.
The participant himself explained the theory of hegemonic masculinity, leaving no interpretive work to the researchers.
The authors excluded his account and diagnosed an identity change solely from independently collected medical records.
items.answer: Licence loss and distress were reported directly; a loss of masculine identity was the authors' qualified interpretation.
items.explanation: Michael described losing his licence, restricted mobility, distress, and the difference between merely surviving and really living. The authors explicitly note that masculine identity loss was not stated by him. That distinction preserves the boundary between his account and their analytical inference; the interview is not an independent clinical assessment.

items.prompt: What does the electric-scooter case illustrate?
options: Walking ability was medically restored, removing every need for assistance or adaptive equipment.
Accepting an aid helped preserve independent mobility and quality of life, reshaping what independence meant.
The scooter prevented access to local shops and medical care, so the participant abandoned independence.
Only masculine self-presentation changed, while the participant's ability to travel and conduct daily life did not.
items.answer: Accepting an aid helped preserve independent mobility and quality of life, reshaping what independence meant.
items.explanation: Arnold used the scooter to visit local services and his doctor on his own despite very limited walking. The authors interpret this as reformulating independence and idealized masculinity through adaptation. His stated range of about 40 km was a capability he said he did not attempt, not a reported routine journey or a verified device specification.

items.prompt: Which practical implication stays within the paper's evidence?
options: Engagement might build on independence and subgroup-specific meanings, with the proposed approach requiring further evaluation.
A standard intervention that suppresses every man's desire for control has already been shown to improve medication adherence.
Universal public health services should be abolished and replaced with private services determined only by chronological age.
Help seeking and treatment participation should be excluded from policy because neither relates to gender or aging identities.
items.answer: Engagement might build on independence and subgroup-specific meanings, with the proposed approach requiring further evaluation.
items.explanation: The authors propose discussing health, treatment, and medication in ways that connect with control, responsibility, and valued independence. They also call for attention to different groups of men and further study of services and relationships. These are practice and policy proposals derived from qualitative accounts, not established intervention outcomes.
